00-Index/Drenthe-Province.title: Drenthe Province
00-Index/Drenthe-Province.content:
Drenthe Province

The ancestral home of the Snoek line.

Geography
Drenthe is a province in the northeast of the Netherlands. It borders:

North: Groningen
East: Germany
South: Overijssel
West: Friesland

Population and emigration
Although Drenthe was the least populated Dutch province in the 19th century, it ranked 4th in number of emigrants to North America. Many Drenthe residents worked in agriculture, so the province was hit particularly hard by crop failures. Many also joined the Secession and were among the first wave of Dutch religious emigrants.
Most Drenthe emigrants settled in:

Holland & Grand Rapids, Michigan
Orange City & Pella, Iowa

”Unwanted elements” colonies
In the 19th century, the Dutch government used Drenthe as a place to relocate so-called “unwanted elements” of society — beggars, vagabonds, and orphans who could not be placed elsewhere were transported to Drenthe to live in colonies and till the land. As a result, people from all over the Netherlands ended up there.
Naming conventions
Most Drenthe residents used patronymics rather than (or in addition to) surnames before 1811, and even for some time after. Drenthe surnames typically end in: -ing[h]e, -in[c]k, -ies, -iens, -heide, -veen. See Dutch-Naming-Conventions.
Snoek family connection
The Snoek line originates from villages in Drenthe:

Roden — birthplace of Arend Snoek (1776–1827)
Zuidlaren — birthplace of Trijntje Eibema (1825–1879)
Gasselte — birthplace of Jan Snoek (1817–1890)
Odoorn — site of Jan Snoek’s marriage to Trijntje (2 May 1846)

Source
Source PDF, page 5; quotation attributed to “Yvette Hitink, 2005.”

00-Index/Dutch-Naming-Conventions.title: Dutch Naming Conventions
00-Index/Dutch-Naming-Conventions.content:
Dutch Naming Conventions

Adapted from the source PDF (pages 2–3). Useful for understanding why so many Adriaansd / Adriaansz / Willemsz suffixes show up in the Snoek and VerBerkmoes lines.

Naming order for children

























































ChildNamed afterFirst sonFather’s fatherFirst daughterMother’s motherSecond sonMother’s fatherSecond daughterFather’s motherThird sonFather’s paternal grandfatherThird daughterMother’s maternal grandmotherFourth sonMother’s paternal grandfatherFourth daughterFather’s maternal grandmotherFifth sonMother’s maternal grandfatherFifth daughterFather’s paternal grandmotherSixth sonMother’s maternal grandfatherSixth daughterFather’s paternal grandmother
Female variations
If no male child was available to name after a grandfather, a daughter often received a feminine version of the grandfather’s given name. Common feminine suffixes:
-je[n] -ke[n] -pje[n] -tge[n] -the[n] -tie[n] -tke[n]
Examples:

Jantje for Jan
Korneliske for Kornelis

Names recycled within a sibling group
Due to high infant mortality, multiple children in a single family often share a name. If a son named after his father died, the next son was again given the father’s father’s name. This continued until either a child survived to adulthood or there were no more children. It is not unusual to see a son born after his father’s death given his father’s name. When a widow remarried, the first son was often named after her deceased husband.
Patronymic suffixes (pre-1811)
Before Napoleon’s 1811 decree forcing surnames, Dutch people used patronymics — a second name derived from the father’s first name. The pattern adds -zoon/-z (son) or -dochter/-d (daughter):

1st generation: Aartzoon
2nd generation: Willem Aartzoon
3rd generation: Aart Reijerzoon (because Aart’s father was Reijer)

This is why VerBerkmoes records show names like Adriaan Willemsz VerBerkmoes (“Adriaan, son of Willem, of the VerBerkmoes family”) and Derkje Adriaansd Schippers (“Derkje, daughter of Adriaan, of the Schippers family”).
Drenthe-specific surname endings
Drenthe surnames typically end in: -ing[h]e -in[c]k -ies -iens -heide -veen
How Napoleon’s 1811 decree played out
When Napoleon decreed that the Dutch must register surnames, the law was designed in part to make it harder for sons to dodge French conscription. The Dutch — “among the greatest saboteurs in the world,” as the source puts it — treated it as a joke and registered some deliberately ridiculous names, expecting the law to be repealed once Napoleon was beaten. It wasn’t, and those names stuck.
The VerBerkmoes line itself illustrates the system: when the law took effect, the family was living at Zwaluwenburg (a “feudal lord” estate meaning “with many managed and fruitful farms”), so they could equally have ended up as “van Zwaluwenburg.”
Common name equivalents





































DutchEnglishJan / Jannes / JohannesJohnTrijntjeCatherine / KaterinaPieter / PeterPeterWillemWilliamAdriaanAdrianKrijn / Krien(no direct equivalent)HendrikHenry
Source
Source PDF, pages 2–3.

00-Index/Home.title: Home
00-Index/Home.content:
Snoek–VerBerkmoes Family Vault
A research vault deconstructed from Ruth Taber’s History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families (timeline document, dated 25 Dec 2025). The original PDF is preserved in _Archive/.

We are the chosen. In each family, there is one who seems called to find the ancestors. To put flesh on their bones and make them live again. We are the storytellers of the tribe.
— Opening of the source document

How this vault is organized

























































FolderWhat lives there00-Index/This Home page, the four family Maps of Content (MOCs), and shared reference notes (Dutch naming conventions, regional geography).01-People/One note per ancestor, organized into family-line subfolders. YAML frontmatter holds birth/death/parents/spouse so the data is queryable.02-Places/Towns, villages, regions — Devon, Hulst, Goes, Roden, Grand Haven, etc.03-Historical-Context/World/national events that shaped the family (Mayflower, French Revolution, Dutch Secession, WWI/II, etc.).04-Local-History/Grand Haven, Spring Lake, Ferrysburg landmarks, businesses, and ships from the timeline.05-Family-Groups/One note per marriage/household. Useful for ahnentafel-style browsing.06-Timeline/Year-indexed stub notes — gives a chronological view of any year.07-Sources/Census records, newspaper clippings, vital records, citations.08-Media/Photographs and scans extracted from the source.09-Research-Log/Open questions, gaps, contradictions, things to follow up on._Archive/The original PDF, untouched._scripts/The Python scripts used to extract this vault from the PDF. Re-runnable; the parsed people.json is also kept here for reference.
Family Maps of Content

MOC-Coffin — English origins (Devon → New England → Wisconsin/Michigan)
MOC-Samargia — Croatian origin (joins the family via Anna Samargia ↔ Clarence Snoek, 1932)
MOC-Snoek — Drenthe origins, settled in Grand Haven, MI
MOC-VerBerkmoes — Zeeland origins, settled in Grand Haven, MI

Each MOC now opens with a direct-line Mermaid ancestry tree (7 VerBerkmoes generations, 8 Coffin generations, 4 Snoek generations, 1 Samargia).
🌳 Interactive family tree

Interactive browser — browse the complete 829-person tree with pan/zoom, ancestor view, descendant view, and hourglass view. Powered by Topola. Loads the GEDCOM below. (Only works via npm run serve/Quartz or any web server; Obsidian’s preview doesn’t run JavaScript.)
GEDCOM export — standards-compliant GEDCOM 7.0 file with 829 individuals and 257 family structures. Import this into Ancestry.com, FamilySearch, MyHeritage, WikiTree, Gramps, Family Historian, RootsMagic, or any other genealogy tool.

Map View
139 place notes have latitude and longitude in their YAML frontmatter. To see the family footprint on a literal map:

In Obsidian: Settings → Community plugins → Browse → search “Map View” → Install → Enable
The config is pre-loaded — it reads latitude/longitude fields and centers on Grand Haven, MI
Open the Map View from the left sidebar (globe icon) or via command palette → “Map View: Open”

Reference notes

Dutch-Naming-Conventions — patronymics, generation rules, why so many “Adriaansd”s
Drenthe-Province — geography of the Snoek homeland
Zeeland-Province — geography of the VerBerkmoes homeland

How to read this vault

Start with a MOC above to get oriented in one family line.
Click any name to open their personal note. From there, parents and spouses are wikilinks — keep clicking to walk the tree.
Use the Graph view (Obsidian’s left sidebar → graph icon) to literally see the family tree as a connected graph. Try filtering by tag — e.g. tag:#snoek shows only the Snoek line.
Use the search (Ctrl+Shift+F) for any name, place, or year.
Add to it. This vault is designed to grow. When you find new sources, drop them into 07-Sources/ and link them from the relevant person notes. When you have a research question, add it to 09-Research-Log/Open-Questions.md.

Status
Phases 1, 2, and 3 of the deconstruction are complete. The vault now covers the entire source PDF.
What’s in the vault now





























































































































SectionCountSourceIndex / reference notes8Home, four MOCs, Dutch naming conventions, province geographyPerson notes836Family group sheets (pp. 165–212) + chronological events (pp. 7–164). Deduplicated via merge_duplicate_people.py — 54 spelling-variant stubs consolidated into their canonical forms.  Coffin38English origins through New England  Snoek42Drenthe → Grand Haven  VerBerkmoes171Zeeland → Grand Haven (largest line)  Samargia1Anna Samargia (1908–2001)  Related584Spouses, in-laws, descendants with other surnamesPlace notes188Normalized canonical place names, organized into country/state subfolders. 139 (73%) have coordinates, 128 (68%) have Wikipedia links.  County hubs502-Places/_Counties/ — Ottawa County MI (6 places, 451 events), Door County WI, Cumberland County ME, Essex County MA, Aa en Hunze NL  Michigan39Grand Haven, Holland, Spring Lake, Ferrysburg, etc.  Netherlands13Zeeland (7) + Drenthe (5) + others  England5Devon (Brixton, Portledge, Alwington)  Other states~115Indiana, Wisconsin, Illinois, Ohio, California, etc.  _Uncategorized20Places lacking state/country infoFamily Group Sheets27105-Family-Groups/ — one note per marriage, with spouses + childrenHistorical-context notes36Mayflower, French Revolution, War of 1812, Dutch Secession, WWI/II, Korematsu, etc. — 100% classifiedLocal-history notes164Grand Haven landmarks, ships, businesses, plus 40+ Dewey Hill newspaper articles by Robert BeatonYear-index notes224One per year from 1535 to 2023 — chronological view of any yearCensus source notes111One per census household, with member lists, parsed roles/ages, raw text preservedEmbedded images276Photos and scans from the source PDF, in 08-Media/, embedded into ~445 notes by source pageResearch log1Open Questions log (4 source typos resolved via corrections overlay)Total markdown notes1,844Total vault size44 MB(30 MB images, 14 MB markdown)
Person-note features
Every person note has:

YAML frontmatter with name, family_line, generation, birth_date, birth_place, death_date, death_place, father, mother, spouses[], tags[], source. Queryable with the Dataview plugin.
Wikilinked parents resolved via fuzzy matching that respects generation, birth year, and middle-name initials, so “Adriaan A Verberkmoes” links to the right gen-6 Adriaan and not his great-grandson.
Wikilinked spouses with their own birth/death info inline.
Auto-computed Children section built from the reverse parent index.
Timeline section (Phase 3a) — chronological events from pp. 7–164 attached to the right person, including censuses, WWII draft cards, immigrations, etc.
Multiple marriages with divorce dates where present.
Source provenance at the bottom of each note (page range + raw “Parents” line if non-trivial, so you can spot OCR or transcription errors).

Place-note features (Phase 3e+)
After the Phase 3 deconstruction, place notes were further consolidated and enriched:

Aggressive normalization — every place string is run through a 6-phase pipeline that strips ages, addresses, person-name leakage, ward/district codes, and county-into-city bleed. State abbreviations and common typos (Wisc/Ill/Ind/Orgon) are expanded. Result: 199 → 189 fully canonical City, State (or City, State, Country) entries.
Curated geo enrichment — for the 47 most-referenced places, _scripts/places_gazetteer.json provides accurate county, state, country, latitude, longitude, wikipedia URL, founding year, and a brief genealogical context note.
County hub notes — 02-Places/_Counties/ contains one note per unique county, aggregating every place + every family event in that county. Ottawa County, Michigan alone aggregates 5 places (Grand Haven, Holland, Spring Lake, Ferrysburg, Nunica) and 441 events.
“Other places in this county” cross-reference on every place note that has a county.
“Local history” and “Census records” sections on every place note, automatically populated from narrative and source notes that match the place name.

Quartz frontend (static site)
A Quartz v4 static-site generator is installed at C:/Users/Heavyarms/Snoek-VerBerkmoes-Quartz/ (outside OneDrive, because node_modules has too many files for OneDrive sync to handle well). It reads this vault directly via the -d flag — no content duplication — and emits HTML with full wikilink graph view, backlinks, full-text search, and dark mode.
Key build facts:

Built site has 1,845 HTML pages (one per note) plus all 276 images, full CSS/JS, sitemap, and RSS feed
Full build takes ~13 seconds (after disabling CustomOgImages)
Site title: Snoek–VerBerkmoes Family History
Custom theme: cream/walnut genealogy-archive palette with Libre Caslon headers

To preview the site locally:
cd C:/Users/Heavyarms/Snoek-VerBerkmoes-Quartz
npm run serve

Then open http://localhost:4321 in your browser. Live-reloads on file changes. Ctrl-C to stop.
To build a static copy (for upload to GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or just zipping to share):
cd C:/Users/Heavyarms/Snoek-VerBerkmoes-Quartz
npm run build

The output lands in C:/Users/Heavyarms/Snoek-VerBerkmoes-Quartz/public/ — fully self-contained static files.
Both npm run serve and npm run build scripts are pre-wired in package.json with the -d flag pointing at this vault, so you don’t have to remember the path.

The vault itself is unchanged by Quartz — you can still open it in Obsidian. Both tools read the same markdown files.

Phase 5 — image extraction
The source PDF contains 276 embedded photos and scans (newspaper clippings, family portraits, ship photos, building photos, ancestry charts). All have been extracted into 08-Media/ and automatically embedded into the relevant notes:

Narrative notes (03-Historical-Context/, 04-Local-History/) embed the image(s) on their source_page.
Census source notes (07-Sources/Census/) embed the image(s) on their source page.
Person notes (01-People/) embed images from every page referenced in their Timeline section. So Clarence Snoek (1905), who has Timeline events on pp. 104, 143, and 149, gets all 11 images from those three pages.

Images are embedded with a 400px width hint and the source page caption. Re-running embed_images.py is idempotent.
Phase 4 — source corrections
A small people_corrections.json overlay file applies hand-curated fixes for the 4 known parent-attribution errors in the source PDF (Ruth Louise Snoek, William VerBerkmoes 1888, Adrian VerBerkmoes 1880, Susan A VerBerkmoes 1881). The original source values are preserved in each affected person note’s footer with a ⚠️ warning marker, so the correction is auditable.
Phase summary























































PhaseStatusWhat it did1✓Vault scaffolding, original PDF preserved in _Archive/2✓631 person notes from family group sheets (pp. 165–212)3a✓615 chronological events extracted; Timeline sections added to 363 existing person notes; ~260 new ancestor notes auto-created (mostly Coffins); 224 year-index stubs3b✓46 historical-context narrative notes3c✓157 local-history notes (Grand Haven landmarks, ships, businesses, Dewey Hill columns)3d✓111 census source notes with parsed household members3e✓302 place notes with consolidated/normalized canonical names4futureBacklink polish + manual merge of any duplicate stubs you spot5futureImage extraction from PDF into 08-Media/
Re-running the extraction
All scripts live in _scripts/ and are re-runnable. If Ruth issues an updated PDF in the future:

Replace the PDF in _Archive/
Re-extract the text:
python _scripts/parse_groupsheets.py
python _scripts/parse_chronological.py
python _scripts/parse_narratives.py


Re-render the notes:
python _scripts/generate_notes.py
python _scripts/generate_narratives.py
python _scripts/generate_sources.py
python _scripts/generate_places.py


Re-extract images and embed them:
python _scripts/extract_images.py
python _scripts/embed_images.py


Run the audit:
python _scripts/audit.py



pypdf and Pillow are the only Python dependencies.
Known limitations to be aware of

A few duplicate stubs may exist — when the source PDF used inconsistent spellings (e.g., "Lizzie" vs "lizzie", Williem vs Willem), the matcher occasionally creates two notes for the same person. Use Obsidian’s “rename and update links” to merge them as you encounter them.
CENSUS events appear only in source notes (07-Sources/Census/), not in the per-person Timeline sections. Each census source note links to its household members, so Obsidian backlinks let you find all censuses for a person.
Source typos — the four known parent-attribution errors are now corrected automatically by the corrections overlay. New typos discovered later can be added to _scripts/people_corrections.json.
Place geo coverage is 25% — 47 of the 191 places have curated geo data (county, coordinates, Wikipedia). The remaining 144 are mostly single-event places. To bring coverage to 100%, run a Wikipedia/Wikidata enrichment script (not yet built — would be Phase 6).

Tristram Coffin (1609–1681) was a founder of Nantucket after emigrating from Butler’s Parish, Brixton, Devon in 1642. The intermediate Coffin generations between Tristram and Stephen are not fully documented in the source.


🌳 Interactive tree: browse the entire 829-person family tree with pan/zoom/ancestor/descendant views at 08-Media/family-tree. A GEDCOM export is also available at 08-Media/snoek-verberkmoes.ged for use with Ancestry.com, Gramps, FamilySearch, or any other genealogy tool.

Origins (Devon, England, 15th century)
The earliest documented Coffins lived at Portledge, Alwington, Devon (Devonshire), and at Butler’s Parish, Brixton, South Hams. The line is documented from around 1425.
Generation outline (early generations from source PDF pp. 7–8)
15th century — founders

Richard Coffin (b. 1425, Portledge, Devon) m. Alice Gambon (b. 1425, Merston, Shropshire) in 1456.
John Coffin (b. 1450, Portledge)

16th century

Sir James Coffin/Coffyn & Mary Ann Cole — parents of Peter Tristram (below)
Peter Tristram Coffin (b. 1535, Portledge, Devon) m. Mary Boscawen (b. 20 Jan 1542, Cornwall) in 1555. Died 16 Nov 1601, Portledge.

Late 16th century

Nicholas Coffin/Coffyn (Nov 1561, Brixton – 5 Oct 1613, Brixton) m. Joan Avent in 1577. Six children incl. Peter, Tristram, Nicholas.

17th century — Mayflower era

Peter Coffin (Coffyn) (b. Jan 1580, Brixton) — son of Nicholas
Tristram Coffin (b. 11 Mar 1609, Butler’s Parish, Brixton) — emigrated to America, became a founder of Nantucket
Dionis Stevens (b. 4 Mar 1610, Brixton, Devon) — wife of Tristram


Tristram Coffin and Dionis Stevens are central early-American figures; their descendants spread through New England and eventually Wisconsin and Michigan.

The line that connects to the Snoeks (19th century, Maine → Wisconsin)

Stephen Coffin & Elisabeth Weston — parents of James R Coffin (b. 17 Jun 1784, Freeport, Cumberland, ME)
James R Coffin (1784 – Feb 1860, Leeds, Androscoggin, ME) — children include Samuel, Nathan, Reuben, George Washington, Elizabeth
Samuel Coffin (1785–1786, infant death) — or a later Samuel; the source has multiple Samuels
Samuel Coffin m. Harriette Smith on 20 May 1837, Isle au Haut, Knox, ME. Six children:

Eliza, David, Martha Ann, Matilda, Clara Barbara, Phoebe


Phoebe Coffin (1847–1935) m. (1) Peter Harder (1830–1879), then m. (2) John Orren Snoek (1817–1890) — the union that joins the Coffin line into the Snoek family.

Mayflower / Pilgrim context
The source document devotes significant space (pp. 8–11) to the Pilgrim migration to Holland and the Mayflower voyage. Tristram Coffin (b. 1609) was born just one year after the first Pilgrim migration to the Netherlands. While he is not a Mayflower passenger himself, he is part of the same generation and emigrated to Massachusetts a few decades later.
To be created in Phase 3:

1620-Mayflower-Voyage

Door County, Wisconsin (1870 — birth of Charles Coffin)

How this MOC was built
The Coffin line is documented heavily in the chronological part of the source PDF (pp. 7–35), not the family group sheets, so most of the early generations don’t yet have individual person notes. Phase 3 will fill in the early Coffins from the timeline.

John Orrin Snoek Sr emigrated from Drenthe to Grand Haven, MI in 1846 with his first wife Trijntje Eibema (1825–1879). 00-Index/Zeeland-Province.title: Zeeland Province
00-Index/Zeeland-Province.content:
Zeeland Province

The ancestral home of the VerBerkmoes line.

Geography
Zeeland (literally “Sea Land”) is the southwestern province of the Netherlands. It is composed of islands and peninsulas in the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta, connected by bridges, tunnels, and the Delta Works flood barriers.
It borders:

North: South Holland
East: North Brabant
South: Belgium

Major towns referenced in the family records include:

Hulst — birthplace of multiple early VerBerkmoes generations
Goes — primary VerBerkmoes town for the 19th century
Borssele — birthplace of Anthonetta Adriana Harinck
Kortgene — birthplace of Derkje Adriaansd Schippers
Middelburg, Vlissingen — major Zeeland cities

The Netherlands and the sea
The Netherlands is a famously flat country — almost 25% of its land is at or below sea level. Over centuries, severe floods devastated the region, killing tens of thousands. The Dutch response was to drain the land using windmills, raise farm and village levels with manmade hills (polders), and eventually dam off the sea entirely. The Afsluitdijk (the great enclosing dike) was built in the early 1930s.
VerBerkmoes family connection
The VerBerkmoes line is documented from the 1680s in Hulst and surrounding Zeeland towns. By the mid-19th century the family was concentrated in Goes, from which they migrated to Grand Haven, Michigan, in 1871 (Elizabeth Johanna Rogge and family).
Key Zeeland-born ancestors:

Adriaan-Willemsz-VerBerkmoes-1821 (born 26 Jan 1821, Goes)
Adriaan-Adriaansz-VerBerkmoes-1849 (born 5 Aug 1849, Goes — emigrated to Michigan)

03-Historical-Context/Gettysburg-Pennsyl.title: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania
03-Historical-Context/Gettysburg-Pennsyl.content:
Gettysburg, Pennsylvania
1863
Traditionally, Abraham Lincoln is viewed as being the man who freed the slaves. A man of immense morals, he is seen as someone whose primary goal in the Civil War was to provide freedom for the slaves in the South. However, a more in-depth analysis is revealed that Lincoln was much more complex that relates the Union back to the foundations of the nation and the principles on which the country was founded. Lincoln maintains that the nation was founded even before the signing of the Declaration of Independence, not the writing of the Constitution.
The immortal words of the Gettysburg Address, “Four score and seven years ago… ” provide the basis for a reefing of the nation as an entity that was and continues to be dedicated to equality. Abraham Lincoln changed the country on that day, just as did the soldiers who fought in that extremely gruesome battle. Lincoln forced people of this country to examine their own morals and principles and begin to understand just a little bit of what true equality means. GETTYSBURG 7,058 soldiers died 3,155 were Union 3.903 were Confederate Brother against Brother Fried against Friend LAKE FOREST CEMETERY GRAND HAVEN MICHIGAN 110 soldiers are buried in Lake Forest Cemetery.
At the time Grand Haven Central Park was the cemetery. Among the soldiers were Major Noah Ferry, who was leading the 5th Michigan Calvary on foot at Gettysburg, when he was fatally shot in the head. Noah’s brother Lt. Col William Ferry Jr.
fought as part of the 14th Michigan Infantry and would later become mayor of Grand rapids and make an unsuccessful run as the Democratic nominee for governor of Michigan. Frederick Graves was born into slavery in Virginia. When the war broke out, he was attached to the Confederate army until he ran away and joined the Union Army. Some African Americans soldiers buried in Grand Haven were part of the 102nd Regiment United States Colored Troops.
To most Americans the Civil War was what we learned in school. The greatest general history may be clear, but the specifics are hard to fathom from present-day perspective. The idea that our nation could literally break in two is happening again in the 2000’s. Had events with the Civil War played our differently, we might be living in a very different world today.
While many aspects of society and culture have changed, it’s important to realize that hopes, dreams and aspirations of Americans back then were very much the same. The destruction of the United States was then, as it would be today, unfathomable and heart breaking. While it is important to consider that every battle that occurred during the Civil War was influenced by events that came before it.

03-Historical-Context/Leaving-Holland-16.title: Leaving Holland
03-Historical-Context/Leaving-Holland-16.content:
Leaving Holland
1620
After deciding to leave Holland, the pilgrims planned to cross the Atlantic using 2 purchased ships. A small ship named Speedwell would first carry them from Leiden to England. The Larger Mayflower would then be used to transport most of the passengers and supplies the rest of the way. Not all of the Separatists were abl e to depart, as many did not have enough time to settle their affairs and their budgets were too meager to buy the necessary travel supplies.
The congregation therefore decided that the younger and stronger members should go first, with others following in the future. Although the congregation had been led by John Robison, who first proposed the idea of emigrating to America. He chose to remain in Leiden and care for those who could not make the voyage. The Pilgrims and Puritans referred to themselves as God’s New Israel’ It was therefore considered the destiny of the Pilgrams & Puritans to similarly build a “spiritual Jerusalem” in America.
When it was time to leave, the ship’s senior leader, Edward Winslow, described the scene of families being separated at the departure: “A flood of tears was poured out. Those not sailing accompanied us to the ship but were not able to speak to one another for the abundance of sorrow before parting. ” William Bradford, another leader who would be the second governor of the Plymouth Colony, similarly described the departure: “Truly doleful was the site of that sad and mournful parting. To see what sighs and sobs and prayers did sound among them, what tears did gush from every eye, and pithy speeches pierced each heart…their Reverend Pastor, falling on hid knees, and they all with him.
” The trip to the south coast of England took 3 days, where the ship took anchor at Southampton on August 5, 1620. From there, the Pilgrams first laid eyes on the larger ship, Mayflower, as it was being loaded with provisions. SPEEDWELL & MAYFLOWER Carrying about 65 passengers, the mayflower left London in Mid-July. The ship then proceeded down the Thames to the south of England, where it anchored at Southampton, Hampshire.
There she waited for the planned rendezvous on July 22 with the Speedwell, coming from Holland with members of the Leiden congregation.
Source

Pilgrams Migrate to the Netherlands

Differing from their contemporary Puritans (who sought to reform and purify the Church of England), the Pilgrams chose to separate from the Church of England, which forced them to pray in private. They believed that its resistance to reform and the Roman catholic past left it beyond redemption. Starting in 1608 a group of 400 English Protestants left England for the Netherlands, where they could worship freely. Life in the Netherlands became increasing difficult for the congregation.
They were forced into menial and backbreaking jobs, such as cleaning wool, which led to a variety of health afflictions. In addition, a number of the country’s leading theologians began engaging in open debates which led to civil unrest, instilling the fear that Spain might again place Holland’s population under siege, as it had done years earlier. England’s King James form an alliance with Holland against Spain, with a condition outlawing independent English church congregation in Holland. These became the separatists motivating factors to sail for the New World, which would have the added benefit beyond the reach of King James and his bishops.

03-Historical-Context/September-16-the-M.title: September 16 the Mayflower Sails
03-Historical-Context/September-16-the-M.content:
September 16 the Mayflower Sails
1620
Western gales turned the North Atlantics into a dangerous place to sail. Mayflower’s provisions were already quite low when departing Southampton, and they became lower still by delays of more than a month. The passengers had been on board the ship this entire time, feeling worn out and in no condition for a very taxing, lengthy Atlantic journey cooped up in the small spaces of a small ship. When Mayflower sailed from Plymouth alone, with what Braford called “a prosperous wind” she carried 102 passengers plus a crew of 25 to 30 officers and men, bringing the total aboard to approximating 130.
At about 180 tons, she was considered a smaller cargo ship, having traveled mainly between England and Bordeaux with clothing and wine, not an ocean ship. Nor was she in good shape, as she was sold for scrap 4 years after her Atlantic voyage. She was a high-built craft forward and after, measuring approximately 100’ in length and about 25’ at her widest point. THE TRIP ACROSS THE ATLANTIC The living quarters for 102 passengers were cramped, with the living area about 20’ x 80’ and the ceiling about 5’ high.
With couples and children packed closely together for a trip lasting two months, a great deal of trust and confidence was required among everyone on board. The first half of the voyage proceeded over calm seas and pleasant skies. Then the weather changed, with continuous northeasterly storms hurling themselves against the ship, and huge waves constantly crashing against the top side deck. In the midst of one storm, William Butten, a young, indentured servant of physician Samuel Fuller, died, the sole fatality of the voyage.
And was buried at sea. A baby was also born, christened Oceanus Hopkins. During another storm, so fiercely that the sails could not be used, the ship was forced to drift without hoisting its sails for days, or else risk losing her masts. The storm washed passaged passenger John Howland overboard.
He sank about 12’ , but and was safely pulled back on board. The passengers were forced to crouch in semi-darkness below deck. With waves tossing the boat in different directions, men held onto their wives, who themselves held onto their children. Water was soaking everyone and everything above and below deck.
In mid-ocean, the ship came close to being totally disabled and might have had to return to England or risk sinking. A storm had so badly damaged its main beam that even the sailors despaired. NOVEMBER 19 ARRIVAL IN AMERICA They sighted present-day Cape Cod. They spent several days trying to sail south to their planned destination of the Colony of Virginia, where they had obtained permission to settle from the Company of merchant Adventures of London.
But the strong winter seas forced them to return to the harbor at Cape Codhook, known today as Provincetown Harbor. And they set anchor on November 21, It was before setting anchor that the male Pilgrims and non-Pilgrim passengers (whom members of the congregation referred to them as “Strangers”) drew up and signed the Mayflower Compact. Among the resolutions in the Compact were those establishing legal order and meant to quell increasing strife within the ranks. Myles Standish was selected to make sure the rules were obeyed, as there was a consensus that discipline would need to be enforced to ensure the survival of the planned colony.
Once they agreed to settle and build a self-governing community, they came to shore. The moment the Pilgrims stepped ashore was described by William Bradford, the second Governor of the Plymouth Colony: “Being thus arrived in good harbor and brought safe to Land, they fell upon their knees and blessed the God of heaven, who had brought them over the vast and furious ocean, and delivered them from all perils and miseries thereof, again to set their feet on the firm and stable earth, their proper element. MONDAY December 7 FIRST WINTER An exploring expedition was launched under the direction of Capt. Christopher Jones to search for a suitable settlement site.
There were 34 persons in the open small boat: 24 passengers and 10 sailors. They were ill-prepared for the bitter winter weather which they encountered on their reconnoiter, as the Pilgrims were not accustomed to winter weather which was much colder than back home. They were forced to spend the night ashore because of the bad weather they encounter, ill-clad in below freezing temperatures with wet shoes and stockings that froze overnight. Bradford wrote, “Some of our people that are dead took the origin of their death here” on the expedition.
Plymouth faced many difficulties during its first winter, the most notable being the risk of starvation and the lack of suitable shelter. The Pilgrims had no way of knowing that the ground would be frozen by the middle of November, making it impossible to do any planting. Nor were they prepared for the snowstorms that would make the countryside impassable without snowshoes. And in their haste, they did not think of bringing fishing rods.
From the beginning, the assistance they received from the local Native Americans was vital. One colonist’s journal reported, “We dug and found some corn, two or three basket full, and a bag of beans. …in all we had about ten bushels, which will be enough for seed. It is with God’s help that we found the corn, for how else could we have done it, without some Indians who might trouble us.
” Governor Bradford held out hope: “Friends, if ever we make a plantation, God works a miracle! Especially considering how scant we shall be of victuals, most of all, united amongst ourselves, and devoid of good tutors and leaders. Violence will break all. Where is the meek and humble spirit of Moses and of Nehemiah, who re-edified the walls of Jerusalem, and the State of Israel?…I see not, in reason, how we shall escape, even the gasping of hunger-starved persons: But God can do much and his will be done.
HOUSES IN THE EARLY PLYMOUTH COLONY The Pilgrims started constructing their living houses and storehouses in late December, but only managed to get a couple built before and during the first winter. They were hindered not only by weather, but by occasional fires usually caused by spark or ember from fire making it onto the dried thatch roof. December 28 50 foot deep lot plots were assigned to 19 family groups. The width of the lot was about 8 feet multiplied by the number of members in the family---so a family would have received a plot approximately 50’ x 48’ .
Each family was responsible for building their own house, as well as supplying labor to build community storehouses, a defensive fort, fences and sheds. Without time, good weather and manpower to quickly build a house, many Pilgrims continued to live on board the Mayflower. The Pilgrims suffered an outbreak of a contagious disease described as a mixture of scurvy, pneumonia and tuberculosis. After it was over, only 53 passengers remained-just half of the crew died as well.
Edward Winslow wrote a letter in December 1621 in which he said, “we have built 7 dwelling houses, and 4 for the use of plantation” . In 1622, they built a fence around the colony for their better defense ----the perimeter was nearly ½ a mile, and the fence was 8-9 feet high. In late 1623, Emmanual Altham wrote that there were about 20 houses, but only 5 were “very fair and pleasant” . By that time, several additional ships carrying passengers, including the Fortune in 1921, and the Anne in 1623 had arrived.
The Fortune brought mostly young, undisciplined men, whom the company hoped would contribute labor. The Anne brought many of the wives and children to the colony who had been left in England . In 1624, Captain John Smith recorded that Plymouth had 32 houses, “where 7 were burnt the last winter” .
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 10.

03-Historical-Context/Stock-Market-Crash.title: Stock Market Crash
03-Historical-Context/Stock-Market-Crash.content:
Stock Market Crash
1929
The “Roaring Twenties” of the previous decade had been a time of industrial expansion in the U S, and much of the profit had been invested in speculation, including stocks. Many members of the public, disappointed by the low By September interest rates offered on their bank deposits, committed their relatively small sums to stockholders. By 1929, the U S economy was showing signs of trouble; the agricultural sector was depressed due to overproduction and falling prices, forcing many farmers into debt, and consumers goods manufacturers also had unsellable output due to low wages and thus low purchasing power. Factory owners cut production and fired off staff, reducing demand even further.
Despite these trends, investors continued to buy shares in areas of the economy where output was declining and unemployment was increasing, so the purchase price of stocks greatly exceeded their real value. By September, more experienced shareholders realized that prices could not continue to rise and began to get rid of their holdings, which caused share values to stall and then fall, encouraging more to sell. As investors panicked, the selling became frenzied. After Black Thursday, leading bankers joined forces to purchase stock at prices above market value, a strategy used during the Panic of 1907.
This encouraged a brief recovery before Black Tuesday. Further action failed to halt the fall, which continued until July 8,1932; by then, the stock market had lost some 90% of its pre-cash value. Congress responded to the events by passing the Banking Acy of 1933 (Glass -Steagall Act), which separated commercial and investment banking. Stock exchanges introduced a practice of suspending trading when prices fell rapidly to limit panic selling.
Scholars differ over the crash’s effect on the Great Depression, with some claiming that the price fluctuations were insufficient on their own to trigger a major collapse of the financial system, with others arguing that the crash, combined with the other economic problems in the U S in the 1920’s, should be jointly interpreted as a stage in the business cycles which affect all capitalist economies.

03-Historical-Context/Treaty-of-Washingt.title: Treaty of Washington
03-Historical-Context/Treaty-of-Washingt.content:
Treaty of Washington
1836
After the Senate ratified the treaty in 1936, Schoolcraft brought it to Mackinac Island for approval by tribal leaders. Over 4,000 Odawa & Ojibway descended upon the island, eager to see the agreement that would keep them in Michigan and provide much needed goods and annuities. When Schoolcraft revealed the treaty to the Anishnaabek were shocked - it was not the same document they signed in Washington. Article II, inserted by the Senate after Anishnaabek leaders departed in 1835, declared that the tribal lands were for only 5 years, “unless the United States shall grant them permission to remain on said lands for a longer period”.
No goods, money or services would be released until the Anishnaabek signed the treaty. The leaders reluctantly signed. With in 2 years, Schoolcraft called for Anishnaabek relocation to Kansas, claiming the Odawa and Ojibway could not be civilized. The Odawa & Ojibway would not leave theirs lands, and fought to remain at the Straits of Mackinac.
The ultimately signed the 1855 Treaty of Detroit, which removed the possibility od forced relocation and kept the Anishnaabek in Michigan. The 1836 Treaty of Washington resulted in the government acquired Anishnaabek land so Michigan could become a state. In addition, the treaty set the stage for self-government by the tribes and established reservations, hunting & fishing rights, and tribal relations with the government. It also stated that the Odawa would have to leave unless they become civilized, and to help them become civilized the government would provide them an annuity and fund school & protestant missions.
1836 Apr Chief Wakazoo petitioned congress for the right to buy land for an agricultural colony near his traditional winter hunting grounds in Allegan County. 1837 Martin Van Buren 8th President of the United States One of the founders of the Democratic Party He was known as the “Little Magician” to his friends & “Sly Fox” to his enemies. He faced financial panic brought about in part by the transfer funds from the Bank of the United States to state banks during Jackson’s second term.

The treaty was signed by Michigan Territorial Governor Lewis Cass, Solomon Sibley for the United States, and the People of Three Fires Chief Meta of the Pottawatomi wanted to appease both demands of his god and the United States: while he believed the Great Spirit wanted him to keep hold of the land, the United States kept asking for more. Either way he feared for the lives of his people. Chief Wakazoo also feared for the lives of his small band Ottawa.
He believed George Smith and Arvilla Powers Smith offered a way out: with Smith’s help the Potawatomi could purchase land from the federal government and learn to become farmers.

03-Historical-Context/Van-Raalte-Leaves-.title: Van Raalte Leaves Buffalo
03-Historical-Context/Van-Raalte-Leaves-.content:
Van Raalte Leaves Buffalo
1846
Van Raalte, with a small part of his party in Buffalo, boarded Ebar B Ward’s Great Western and steamed toward Detroit for a three-day journey. Their fare was $6.50 for crossing Lake Erie. They had 3 meals a day. Van Raalte was struck by how fast Americans ate, that meat was served at every meal and how few vegetables were eaten.
They had beef steak, read, coffee or tea, and unpeeled potatoes, small helpings of vegetables and many other unfamiliar dishes. No deference was given because of social class, and people paid little attention to how well others were dressed. Anyone who could pay his way was an equal’ People were hospitable, but Van Raalte heard few compliments. He also noted with interest the number of individuals who read newspapers.
1846 Mon Nov 30 At Detroit, Van Raalte’s party learned that since it was late in the season, the Great Lakes were freezing and no boats would leave for Milwaukee until spring. Traveling by land was too expensive since the railroads did not extend to Kalamazoo. Van Raalte found rooms for his family, but the poor Dutchmen traveling with him were divided. Some found shelter in a Detroit warehouse; ten families accepted E B Ward’s offer to work on a steamboat he was building at St.
Clair, in exchange for room and board. Since these Dutch immigrants had few skills and didn’t understand English, they were assigned the most menial tasks. At the same time Detroit was the state capital. When state leaders learned of Van Raalte’s plan to establish a Dutch Colony, they urged him to consider Michigan rather than continue to Wisconsin.
Michigan was anxious for settlers. The state’s growth had been slowed by financial fiasco created when its internal improvements plan collapsed. The state was discredited when it repudiated its bonds without transportation. Few people moved into the interior.
Ships sailing from Detroit through the straits often continued to the western side of Lake Michigan since there were more settlements in Wisconsin and Illinois. Van Raalte was both befriended and strongly influenced by Detroit attorney Theodore Romeyn, a descendent of early Dutch settlers in the east. He had ties to the Reformed Church and spoke Dutch. Van Raalte was also aided by the Reverend George Duffield of the Presbyterian Church.
Some of their argument were legitimate; others were balderdash. Michigan maintained close ties with eastern markets that would strengthen as roads were developed and railroads completed. On the other hand, western trade would be tied to the Mississippi River and New Orleans, where slavery would be confronted. Western Wisconsin had few settlements, making travel and trade difficult; eastern Wisconsin had a mixed population of immigrants that might be indifferent towards the religious Netherlands.
Michigan, however, was populated by old settlers from the East who were more scholarly, enterprising, and religious. They would appreciate and respect Dutch immigrants. Michigan forest lands would be inexpensive to farm and would provide more building materials than the prairie. Michigan was healthier, for the southern Wisconsin climate was too hot for immigrating Hollanders.
Van Raalte was convinced to at least explore sites in Michigan. The good domine was introduced to Allegan judge John Kellog, who jumped at the opportunity to show him. As 1846 drew to a close, Kellog led Van Raalte on an exhausting 11-day trek through deep snow, examining sites in Kent, Allegan and Ottawa Counties. As soon as he saw it, Van Raalte was convinced that the east Black Lake, present day Lake Macatawa, was the ideal location for his kolonie.
The lake emptied into Lake Michigan so it would make a good harbor. He was not a farmer, but thought the sandy soil was similar to his homeland. The forest would be easy to clear, and the wood would be useful for construction and fuel. The location was relatively isolated so the immigrants would not be disrupted by outsiders But Grand Haven, Allegan, and Grand Rapids were near enough to provide supplies.
Only three buildings stood in the area: the cabin of Isaac Fairbanks, the frame house of the Reverend George Smith and a mission church for the three hundred Ottawa Indians who lived in the nearby wigwam village called Niwegah or Old Wing. Most of these Indians, led by chief Waukazoo, had been converted to Catholicism by French priests, but the United States government had sent Smith, a Congregational missionary, to assimilate the Ottawa, while Fairbanks taught them to farm. The Indians had relinquished most of their lands by treaty and received a pension of about $8.00 a year. They lived peacefully, trying to retain their traditions and follow time-tested practices and generally ignoring Smith and Fairbanks’ efforts.
Once he had decided upon this site, Van Raalte moved quickly. Traveling north he met with the Reverend William ferry, founder of Grand Haven, then returned to Detroit with Judge Kellog. A committee of seven prominent Michiganians was formed, who pledged themselves to aid Dutch immigrants moving west and the help Van Raalte secure land. His funds had dwindled to four hundred dollars, so the committee bought land from the state and federal government and held it in trust.
Three thousand acres were obtained on credit from a family living in New York. potential sites in western Michigan where tracts of land were still available for reasonable prices
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 38.

03-Historical-Context/Wounded-Knee-Massa.title: Wounded Knee Massacre
03-Historical-Context/Wounded-Knee-Massa.content:
Wounded Knee Massacre
1890
The U S Army surround a Lakota Sioux encampment in South Dakota during a tense disarmament. A shot fired, and chaos erupted as soldiers opened fire wife rifles and Hotchkiss guns. By the end, more than 300 Lakota men, women and children were killed. Remembered as the Wounded Knee massacre, it marked the violent end of the Indian Wars and stands as one of the darkest chapters in American history.
In the chaos of the massacre, some 25 members of the 7th Calvary were killed, most of whom died as a result of gun fire from their own troops occupying positions on the opposite side of the clearing were their victims. Forsythe attempted to describe the massacre as a battle, but investigations of witnesses revealed otherwise and he was later stripped of his command only to have it reinstated and his men receive awards for bravery. It was part of a political spin on the incidents so as to vilify the 7 th Cavalry and to continue the narrative of the militant cult growing amongst the Lakota, known as the Ghost dancers. 20 members of the 7th Cavalry even receive the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest award for valor in the United States Armed Forces, for their actions.
The massacre was the last major confrontation between the US Army and the Native American tribes. Believing that only death would follow if they didn’t summit, many chiefs encouraged assimilation into the white man’s world. The Ghost Dancers disappeared after the failure of Jesus to descend from Heaven in 1891.
Source

04-Local-History/Barque-Isabella-Arrives.content:
Barque Isabella Arrives in the Port of New York
1846
After 61 days at sea, the Isabella arrived in the Port of New York. Another child on the ship died while the ship was in port. With snow on the ground, the passengers debarked the ship, spent the night in New York, and traveled by train to Albany the next day rather than by boat because of the ice on the Hudson River. They arrived in Albany late in the day.
Because of ice, the ferry boat was not operating so they walked over river on the ice and moved into an over-crowed hotel. Many slept under tables or in chairs. Luggage for many of them arrived two days later. While waiting for word from Domine A.
C. Van Raalte they found work in the area.

04-Local-History/Barque-Isabella-Jan-Tri.content:
Barque Isabella — Jan & Trinjtje Snoek departed the Barque Isabella 1846 Dec 3…
1846
Jan & Trinjtje Snoek departed the Barque Isabella 1846 Dec 31 Arville Smith’s side of the story Judge Kellogg, of Allegan, took Dominie Van Raalte to our Old Wing Mission. Our first thought was: “Praise God, help us with our mission. After an introduction, Judge Kellogg informed us: “Mrs. Smith, Mr.
Van Raalte will remain as your guest and Mr. Smith, you should assist the Dominie in his work. This was a sudden surprise. Mr.
Smith and I had labored under so many disadvantages and had to practice the most rigid economy to build and finish our house for the winter. When that was accomplished, we were hoping for a little enjoyment and rest in our cozy house. My health was frail, and I had no help but my little girls, and Mr. Smith had to be doctor, teacher and preacher to the Indians.
We bowed and bent and turned to the Lord for help. After December Mr. Van Raalte became an established member of our family. I had his washing in addition to my own family’s and was soon so over-worked that I was but a shadow of myself.
Mr. Smith had to roam the woods through the deep snows, and sometimes had to drag the Dominie home, and into the house would a wailing cry, “Oh, Mrs. Smith, I can do no more”. He remained with us for six weeks and then went to Allegan.
After a rest of a few days, we were very sensibly surprised by his return, bring with him two Holland families, and a number of men. They took possession of our nicely furnished parlor, and a cook store was erected, barrels and boxes brought in and instead of being the master and mistress of the situation, we found that we must be in submission to them. We gather enough dishes to set our table for breakfast at 9 o’clock, dinner at 2, and supper at 8 We were cheerful in sacrifice. We were doing the Lord’s work in helping a Christian people to erect their humble homes in a new country .
When the spring came, we were left to say “Amen”. But not so with Mr. Van Raalte. He thought he would have his family come and occupy the best part of the house while he erected a dwelling for them.
Mr. Smith thought differently, so they agreed to disagree, and we were minus even thanks. There were many unacceptable and irreparable marks left in our parlor besides. But afterward, I am thankful to say that our services were duly appreciated by the Dominie and his family.
Through it all, the Smiths and the Odawa remained close. Arvilla’s daughter, Mary. Married Old Chief Joseph Wakazoo’s nephew, 1847 Late January Property was secured and Van Raalte prepared a place for his flock and other immigrants arriving from New York. The ten families living in St.
Clair were contacted and told they could be the first to move to the new site. Six pounced upon the opportunity, gathered their goods and moved to Detroit. 1847 Friday Feb 5th Aided by Romeyn, they boarded a Michigan Central train and arrived in Kalamazoo. Members of the Presbyterian Church sheltered for the night and arranged for sleighs to transport them to Otsego and then to Allegan where Van Raalte and Kellog waited.
They arrived on Saturday, rested on the Sabbath, then met on Monday to discuss their course of action. The women and children remained in Allegan while 5 men - E Zagers, E Frederiks, H Lankheet, J Laarman and W Notting, whose wife accompanied them as cook-traveled with Van Raalte to Holland to construct shelters for the families. After traveling by an ox drawn sleigh over a primitive road blazed through the forest, they arrived at Smith’s Old Wing. Van Raalte stayed with Smith; the others slept on the floor of Fairbanks’ cabin for the next two weeks.
With the help of two hired American workers, they cut a road northward from the mission until they reached the cedar swamps along the Black River. After raising a 16x30 foot cabin, they sent for their families. Six families crowded into that first shanty. A second shelter was begun for other families, expected soon.
The first settlers were Evert Zagers, W. Notting and his wife, Hermanus Lamkheet, Egbert Fredericks, and Mr. and Mrs. Grootenhuis.
1847 Tuesday Feb 9th Founding of the Dutch settlement which was called Holland, Michigan. Holland, the Centertown, was laid out and the lots sold, but those who arrived as intact congregations with their own domine chose outlying sites. Part of the Isabella group left Albany in the middle of February by train to Buffalo. They traveled on foot to Detroit, then by train to Kalamazoo, and finally by sleigh to the new colony of Holland.
The first religious worship was held in the open air. Expecting to find a promise land, the Dutch migrants found instead a swamp and insect-infested forest. Food was a pressing problem, and the log sheds they built were unable to hold everyone, the settlers persevered. Wheat bran and corn was the standard fare.
There were no stoves, so the cooking had to be done over an open fire, with bread being rolled into balls and baked in the ashes, and a brew of roasted corn substituting for tea and coffee. Van Raalte realized the practical and economic potential of the dense forest trees could be felled to build homes and businesses, while the excess lumber could be sold to purchase farming supplies. The rest of the group remained in Albany and worked odd jobs and waited for word from Van Raalte. Mar 10 As the rest of Van Raalte’s original party still waited to come, 15 others arrived and moved into the second cabin.
Upon learning that another group was coming from St Louis, the men tried to build a shelter at the mouth of Black Lake. They gathered boards from the deserted town site of Superior and along the Lake Michigan shoreline, but the work had to be abandoned because there were no nails. Often the falling trees injured the inept axman or crushed the shelters they were constructing. The situation improved once hired American workmen showed them how to clear the forest.
Organizing work and assigning responsibilities also proved difficult. In Holland’s early history, Van Raalte was a spiritual leader, as well as overseeing political, education and financial matters. Van Raalte established a congregation of the Reformed Church of America, which would later be called the First Reformed Church of Holland.
Source

04-Local-History/Before-the-Grand-Haven-.title: Before the Grand Haven Fire
04-Local-History/Before-the-Grand-Haven-.content:
Before the Grand Haven Fire
1889
Washington Ave Grand Haven, MI Culter House Hotel was one of many buildings burnt to the ground. Culter lost both his home and the hotel. 1889 Oct 1 The fire appears to have started at 1:00 that morning at Mull’s Meat market, where an overhead chimney or a fire from a rendering kettle. The building was wood framed and adjacent to the Culter House and quickly spread to Slayton Grocery Store and Henry Baar’s Drug Store.
The fire department was soon on the scene, but strong winds intensified the flames, spreading them to adjoining buildings, mostly to the east and northeast. The mansard roof of the Culter House caught fire. The guests were awakened and evacuated in their night clothes. No lives were lost, but many visitors lost their personal belongings and possessions.
Embers flying across the street ignited the First Reformed Church, which burned to the ground, along with its parsonage. The magnetic Mineral Springs on the northwest corner of Third & Washington was spared. The fire destroyed dozens of homes and buildings, despite the help of the Spring Lake, Grand Rapids and Muskegon fire companies. A total of 52 structures were destroyed or severely damaged, and about 500 people were left homeless.
After its buildings were destroyed he First Reformed Church was left with a 1700 debt from the previous church building, the membership forged forward. A similar structure was built on the same foundation at the cost of 12,224, and a parsonage was built next door for $3000. This 4th church building was 60’ wide & 100’ long with 2 entrances on the southwest corner. A large lecture room & gallery occupied the front of the building on the Washington St.
side and a pulpit was in the exreme north end.

Deboe
1907
‘S CONFECTIONARY Grand Haven, MI DeBoe moved his store to 108 Washington, and eventually had his candy stand in a corner of the Hostetter News at 135 Washington. Although DeBoe’s candy recipes were from a book, Grand Haven area residents tasted something special in his confections. DeBoe claimed it was a cooking process. During WWI, WWII and the Korean War, enlisted servicemen wrote requesting, Pete’s fudge be sent “because the stuff we get here doesn’t taste like his” According to Marie Snoek, after Pete’s wife died in a fire, Aunt Phoebe Snoek thought he would marry her, but it never happened.
THE PANIC OF 1907 Also known as the 1907 Banker’s Panic or Knickerbocker Crisis, was a significant financial crisis in the United States that occurred over a 3-week period starting mid-October. During this time, the New York Stock exchange experienced a dramatic decline, falling nearly 50% from its peak the previous year. The panic was characterized by widespread banks runs and collapse of several financial institutions, leading to significant contraction in the economy. Speculative investments, liquidity issues and lack of a central bank.
The panic began with the collapse of the Knickerbocker Trust Company, which was New York’s 3rd largest trust. JP Morgan’s Intervention: The financier played a crucial role in managing the crisis by organizing a coalition of bankers to provide liquidity to struggling institutions. His actions helped restore some confidence in the federal system. The panic had far-reaching effects on the U S financial system.
It highlighted the need for a central banking system to manage liquidity crisis and prevent future panics. 1907 Mar 4 First Reformed Church Kalamazoo, MI Peter VerBerkmoes 20y received in full communion Son of Adrian & Elizabeth J Rogge VerBerkmoes Dismissed to the 2nd Reformed Church Jul 30, 1909 1907 Jun 8 4th FIRST REFORMED CHURCH FIRE Grand Haven, Michigan A portable heater placed in the back of the organ to dry it out caught fire and destroyed the whole building.

Glorious Fourth Dewey Hill Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Daily Tribune Grand haven should have the biggest Fourth of July celebration in the history of the town this year. We must begin early and make it a howler.
Major Mansfield makes some good suggestions which would be well for the arrangement committee to follow. One suggestion is to have a display of the mammoth fishing industry of Grand Haven. This could be arranged on the city’s riverfront. Have the twelve or more fish tugs of the port gaily decorated and steam up and down the river in a line.
The tygs can be followed by fishing smacks and sail boats. If possible, all the crafts in port could take part and add to the display. A net could be placed in the river, and the fishermen show methods of hauling in the catch. People from the country and interior towns would be interested in such a display.
People who live in lake ports all their lives little know what fascination the lake and vessels have for the interior residents. Excursions could be run several miles in the lake and also up the river and to Spring Lake and Fruitport Last, but by no means least, the pleasure and entertainment of the day should end with a grand military and naval display on the river. The display of 2 years ago was a marvel of all the visitors to the city. Nothing like it had ever been seen in Grand Haven.
It was a grand sight and should be repeated this year, only on a grander scale if possible. Big bon fires should be lit on top of the hill and on the sides, the military and batteries arranged so as to show off effectively, and fireworks. Then let a gun boat proceed down the river. It to be bombarded by the batteries on the hill and replying with its own guns.
Have the spars and rigging of the vessel, so arranged so that when it catches fire it will show off with proper effect. Major Mansfield also suggests that a mine exploded on the hill. It could be located about in the center and enough space in it to remind one of Petersburg when it exploded.
Source

Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune An old settler, while in a reminiscent m
1897
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune An old settler, while in a reminiscent mood the other day, said that the big sand hill across the river, which will always be our most important landmark, if it could tell its secrets of its bosom, would unfold many a mystery and interesting story. Old Indians legends prove that in very early times, in the period about 1730, this hill was held in deep veneration by the aborigines. That was fully a 100 years before the eyes of white men rested upon it. In those times the big hill was used for signaling post and great fires on its peak would often light up the forests for miles around.
This hill, and Baldhead Mountain near Saugatuck, were celebrated in Indian legend from time immemorial. One of the most celebrated Chieftains of the early days of the century, Mequsgon, is buried in this monument of sand. He was a fried of the white man and as early as 1820 predicted that the red race would be entirely exterminated within 100 years. Coming to later times we are told that the sands of the old hill covered many barrels of whiskey, which were being smuggled through the county and hidden there in order to prevent revenue officers from capturing it.
Source

Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune Grand Haven celebrated the nation’s birt…
1894
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune Grand Haven celebrated the nation’s birthday yesterday in a way it never did before. Ten thousand visitors were in town and helped the eagle scream. The day was ushered in by the usual ringing of bells at sunrise and the national salute was fired by the guns of Fox Battery. Excursion trains brought in the visitors early and at the hour of procession the streets were lined with the multitude.
The parade was the grandest ever attempted in Grand Haven and its magnificence surprised even the committee who had it in charge. It started down Washington St., at 11:00 with Marshall of the day VanderVeen, on his old charger in the lead. …Immediately after the parade the militia were hustled down to the waterfront and transported across the river to the big hill where the land naval battle was to take place. Seen from the dock it was a beautiful sight.
Halfway up the hill was the fort with the flag of the Republic floating above it. At the very top of the hill was a party of men signaling to the troops below. One of the big guns of the Fox Battery was located near the electric plant and the other across the river. The Life Saver’s gun was across the river.
Troops were stationed on ridges opposite each other, and the fireworks were sent up from all parts of the hill. When the battle began the scene was one of grandeur. The big guns belched forth as fast as they could be loaded and the echo in the hill reverberated a minute afterwards. A search light from the electric plant displayed the movement of the troops and cast a beautiful shadow on the hill.
The flash of the militiamen’s rifles could be seen and a second or two later the report would be heard on the other side of the river. The volley from the whole squad of troops would follow. A rebel privateer comes floating down the stream, is fired upon, and returns the fire. The hill battalions are firing upon the vessel and soon it is in Flames.
The burning, booming cannons, rattling of the musketry and the varied lights and fireworks formed a scene, which all who witnesses will not soon forget. The throng on this side of the river was sorry when it was over, and after the return of the troops to the city, most of them left for their homes satisfied with the celebration and ready to come another year.
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 86.

Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune If poplar trees grow on the beach at the…
1899
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune If poplar trees grow on the beach at the Park, why won’t they grow on Dewey Hill? The sandy face of the big sand hill should be planted with these trees. Poets have sung of the beauties of Italian skies and Italian sunsets; painters have tried to make the canvas speak what the eye had seen, but right opposite Grand Haven is as pretty a scene as a poet ever dream of or Painter ever attempted to picture. It is the sunset and moonrise as seen from Dewey Hill.
The other evening a party of our citizens viewed this grand spectacle, and the picture will be retained in their mind’s eye for all time. It was an August evening and only a light breeze from the east stirred the hot air. The huge fiery sun sank in the golden glory of the western sky behind old Lake Michigan; its mellow rays shot athwart the heavens and slowly faded into deeper hues, then out of site entirely. A field of crimson marked the sun’s descending place and twilight deepened over the beautiful Grand River valley to the north and east.
Far away in the hazy blue of eventide an occasional light could be seen; gradually the lights increased in number, which told of the descent of night. The darkness was brief. Across The valley stretching away to the east, came the rays of the moon, the light filling every cervice in all the open spaces. As night settled a cool night breeze came up and in the bright moonlight one could fairly see the ripples of the lake.
The hills and valleys seemed flooded with light as far as one could see. The branches of the smaller trees along the ridge of the hill bent mournfully in the night breeze, while the summer winds seemed to chant a dirge through the blasted branches of the veteran trees tops toward Sleepy Hollow. It was a grandly beautiful scene.
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 98.

1899
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune If some inventive Yankee would devise an instrument that could detect buried whiskey, there would be a fortune for him right here in Grand Haven. Over the sands of Dewey Hill, about 50 years ago were buried 16 barrels of choice Bourbon whiskey. Although a few feeble attempts have been made to find this whiskey, all searches so far have been of no avail. This whiskey was brought to Grand Haven by a schooner that was wrecked on the north side of the harbor entrance.
Story has it that the schooner was a filibuster and that the whiskey was taken from Canada. Rix Robinson got possession of the wet goods and at once took steps to hide it. He buried all but one barrel in the big hill, and it is still there. Rix, years after it was buried, told several of our older settlers where it could be found.
In the course of these years a great amount of sand has drifted over the barrels. But the whiskey in its secure hiding place is getting better and better every day and it is figured by those who know that each one of the 16 barrels hidden in the sands of old Dewey Hill will be worth 1200 or 1500 each to the finder… 1900’s INEQUALITY DURING THE GILDED AGE The Progressive Era preceded by the Gilded Age, which today summons images of titled top hats and enormous East Coast estates. But for the vast majority of Americans, it was an era of poverty, as a handful of robber barons ran up unfathomable fortunes by dominating burgeoning industries, often aided by rampant corruption and the exploitation of workforces with few legal protections. Big business was suddenly hundreds of times bigger than it had ever been before, and the Progressive Era legislation aimed to stop it crushing American society under its weight.

Second, that it is the duty of the United States to demand, and the government of the United States does hereby demand that the government of Spain at once relinquish its authority and government in the island of Cuba and withdraw its land and naval forces from Cuba and Cuban waters. Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune Our Samson Celebration Grand Haven did i
1898
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune Our Samson Celebration Grand Haven did itself proud last night to celebrate the glorious naval victory of Admiral Sampson, and outrivaled any previous patriotic celebration ever held in Western Michigan. It was one of the unique affairs incidentals to this Spanish war and will go down in local history and will be spoken of and remembered for many years to come. … …The fun began shortly after 7 o’clock, when every whistle in the city was blown and every bell was rung. The din could only have been heard to be appreciated.
Suffice it to say that farmers 20 miles away heard the noise. The bang of firecrackers and of Doddington’s battery contributed to the general uproar… …At the close of the speaking the crowd was accorded the great American privilege of hurrahing the different popular heroes and leaders and the cheers and tigers were heard in Nunica. After singing the national hymn, the meeting was dispersed, and everybody proceeded to the river to witness the spectacular part of the night’s hot time. On the way to the dock the band headed the procession followed by the High School Cadets, who as they marched along, fired Roman candles into the air.
This made a very pretty sight. All the time the Doddington cannon handled by Wallace Doddington was booming away at a lively rate and the crowd, several thousand strong was pouring down to the Goodrich and D & M dock to secure points of advantage to better witness the fireworks display on Dewey Hill. The fireworks display on the big sand hill was fine and the rockets and candles were varied and pretty. During the firing of rockets and candles, the Goodrich and Crosby liners, the Fanny M.
Rose and every other boat on the river opening their whistles and made a frightful din. At 10 o’clock the evening’s celebration was finished and the crowds dispersed …and Grand Haven’s greatest patriotic demonstration was at an end.

1898
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune Sampson and Victory The grand victory of Admiral Samson in the Caribbean Sea will be celebrated in Grand Haven tonight by the grandest demonstration of the kind ever attempted here. The public generally will take part and make night a unique one in local history… …On the hill opposite the D & M depot, which is hereafter to be known as Dewey Hill, will occur the spectacular part of the night’s fun. The big sand mountain will be alive with fireworks and at a given signal a monstrous pile of boxes and inflammable matter will be touched off at the top of the hill and grand Haven people will have the pleasure of seeing the most monstrous bon fire they ever saw. The blaze, at the very crest of old Dewey hill will illuminate the county for miles and will be distinguishable all the way up the Grand River valley to Grand Rapids.
The celebration of tonight was held at very short notice but when we proposed everybody jumped at it. Boxes and wood were contributed by merchants and citizens, and an army of boys was employed in carrying this material from the bottom to the top of the hill. Everyone worked with a will and tonight Grand Haven will show Michigan and the outside world what a patriotic little city she is.

1898
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune The Fourth of July celebration was actually quite small compared to that of 1891, 1894, 1899. However, the news of Admiral William T. Sampson’s destruction of the Spanish fleet at Santiago, Cuba on July 3rd reached Grand Haven on the 4th and a large impromptu celebration was had on the 5th.
