04-Local-History/Dewey-Hill-Grand-Haven-.title: Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune WAR DECLARED BY SPAIN At 11:00 today the…
04-Local-History/Dewey-Hill-Grand-Haven-.content:
Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune WAR DECLARED BY SPAIN At 11:00 today the…
1898
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune WAR DECLARED BY SPAIN At 11:00 today the Spanish Government declared war against our country, and Minister Woodford was ordered to leave Spain. The flying squadron id headed for sea and all preparations are made to bombard Havana. Spain claims that our demand is entirely unjust, and her only recourse is to fight. Excitement is great throughout the country and companies of volunteers are being organized.
The war spirit was rampant all-over Grand Haven yesterday afternoon and last evening. At 2:30 the news reached here that Spain had practically declared war by giving Minister Woodford his passports. Acting upon these advice a grand demonstration was held by the factories at closing time, at 5:30. Every factory whistle in town was blown, the bells were ringing, downtown some of the patriotic shot firecrackers and the din which commenced at 5:30 continued until 6.
It was the greatest patriotic celebration of its kind ever had in this city. People in the country districts, seven or eight miles from town heard the noise of the whistles and thought a great fire was prevailing. The excitement occasioned brought many people into the streets last night and there was considerable war talk. At 8:30 the high school boys with several hundred followers marched up and down the street to music of fife and drum.
At their head was a flag bearer with a handsome American flag. The boys sang patriotic airs, shot firecrackers in Central Park, blew up the effigy of a Spanish Don with the biggest cannon cracker that could be found. Then followed more singing and marching, and Grand Haven’s first big Spanish war night was over. A fire on the big sand hill contributed to the celebration here last night.
On the occasion of the first American victory, it has been proposed that a monster fire be built there. It could be seen for mils around. If anyone doubted Grand Haven’s patriotism, their doubts were soon dispelled last evening. Pent-up enthusiasm was let loose in one mighty roar and in the hours between 5 and 9 pm there was more noise the Fourth of July.
1898 Mon Apr 25 - Fri Aug 12 SPANISH AMERICAN WAR During the Spanish American War, the company temporarily became part of the 32nd Regiment of the Michigan Volunteer Infantry. The company served briefly in Florida, and saw no action in Cuba, and returned to Grand haven on September 24, 1898. 1898 May 1 In the early hours of the morning, Commodore George Dewey led a US naval squadron into manila Bay in the Philippines. He destroyed the anchored Spanish fleet in 2 hours before pausing the Battle of Manila Bay to order his crew a second breakfast.
In total, fewer than 10 American seamen were lost, while Spanish losses were estimated at over 370. Manila itself was occupied by U.S. troops by August. The elusive Spanish Caribbean fleet was located in Santiago harbor in Cuba.
An army of regular troops and volunteers under General William Shafer (including then-former assistant sectary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt and his 1st Volunteer Cavalry, the ‘Rough Riders”) landed on the coast east of Santiago and slowly advanced on the city in an effort to force Cervera’s fleet out of the harbor. Cevera led his squadron out of Santiago on July 3 and tried to escape westward along the coast. In the ensuing battle all his ships came under heavy fire from U.S. guns and were beached in a burning or sinking condition.
Santiago surrendered to Shafter on July 17, thus effectively ending the brief but momentous war. A combination of savvy public relations and racial bias overemphasized the 40-year-old Roosevelt’s combat role, while downing playing the bravery and contributions of the Black troops, known as Buffalo Soldiers, who served alongside white soldiers on the same battlefield. In his book about the war, Roosevelt called them “shirkers” . But for many historians, they stand among the hardest fighting heroes of the three-week-war.
In their push to capture the strategically important city of Santiago de Cuba, some 8,000 Americans battled for the nearby hills pf San Juan Heights, including Roosevelt’s volunteer regiment and some 1250 Black soldiers. Unlike in most wars, the fighting was an integrated effort. “Regulars and volunteers, black s and whites, fought side by side, endured the blistering heat and driving rain, and share food and drink as well as peril and discomfort, ” wrote U.S. defense Department historian Frank “They forged a victory that did not belong primarily to Teddy Roosevelt, nor did it belong mainly to the Buffalo soldiers.
It belonged to all of them. ” The report as translated read as follows: “Manila. May 1----The squadron arrived at Manila at daybreak this morning. We immediately engaged the enemy and destroyed the following Spanish vessels: Reina Christina, Castilla, Uila, Isle, DeCuba, General Lezo, Duero, Correo, Velasco, Mindenao, on transit, and the battery at Cavite.
Our squadron is uninjured, and a few men were slightly injured. ” Later advice are that only six men were slightly wounded and that Dewey’s forces were not sufficient to make a landing in Manila, but that this in no way interferes with the complete control he exercises over the city and fortifications. It is stated that Dewey silenced the batteries and cut the cable himself, but on account of lack of men did not venture to take his crew ashore. Another cable says that the Spaniards lost 400 killed and 600 wounded The whistles should blow, the guns should boom, and the bells should ring tonight because of the victory by Dewey.
Let the victory of Dewey be celebrated tonight and let the small boy give vent to his enthusiasm to his heart’s content. Grand Haven, Michigan At 9:30 this morning the navy department at Washington received the glorious news from Admiral Dewey of his splendid victory in Manila. It was date Hong Kong and was in cipher. It was brief but right to the point.
Source

Dewey Hill — Grand Haven Tribune What would have been the grandest celebr…
1899
Grand Haven, MI by Robert Beaton Grand Haven Tribune What would have been the grandest celebration in history of Grand Haven was spoiled by rain. But for the elements we would have had the largest crowd in years. It started to rain Monday night, and the dampness continued all through the Fourth without a let up. The oldest residents cannot remember when we had a fourth just like it.
Everyone was disappointed. The parade had to be dispensed with and so also the exercises in Central Park. The committee on parade had provided for a splendid parade and it was with regret that it had to be thrown up. None, however, could be expected to turn out in the steady downpour.
The ardor of all was damped and of a lot of sports on the program, only the bicycle races were held. This road race was one of the redeeming features of a horrible day. Despite the weather, an excursion load of 400 people came to town on one train alone and there were farmers here. If it were a perfect day, 8,000 strangers would have spent the day with us.
As it was, the different places of refreshment did fairly well and many a dollar was put in circulation…

Ferrysburg, Michigan
1864
Johnston Boiler Works John Watt Johnston, a direct descendant of James Watt, the steam engine pioneer, purchased the defunct Turnbull Boiler Works in Ferrysburg. The Turnbull factory, sitting dormant for 2 years, was strategically located at the mouth of the Grand River. Johnston was attracted to the sounds of lumberjack saws and axes at work. Since he was involved in harvesting the lumber and transporting it to market, it was the only logical solution was to be part of the next step taken with lumber construction.
Shortly after shipbuilding became a Johnston product, boiler operations were expanded to design, develop and manufacture a new line of steam generators for the use in construction machinery.

Fire in the Commerce Building
1921
Destroying the 1890 Federal Census Records In the late afternoon , an employee noticed smoke rising through the elevator shaft and sounded the fire alarm. For hours, firefighters soaked the building with water to quench the flames. When the smoke cleared, archives found 25% of the 1890 Census schedules destroyed, while half of the rest sustained serious damage. Government officials debated whether the burnt and water logged records could be salvaged.
The fire originated in the basement of the commerce building and 5 alarms quickly brought every piece of apparatus in downtown Washington to the scene and more the 20 lines of hose completed the damage done to the records by pouring tons of water through windows into vaults where the records were kept.

04-Local-History/Grand-Haven-Officially-.title: Grand Haven Officially Named
04-Local-History/Grand-Haven-Officially-.content:
Grand Haven Officially Named
1835
The Post Office of Grand Haven was located in the Ferry building on Water St. now Harbor Dr. THE FIRST SCHOOL IN GRAND HAVEN The first public school was erected on Lot 186, the east side of Second St between Washington and Franklin- approximately 18 South Second St. The building was owned by Rev.
William M Ferry. It was one a one room frame structure that served as a general meeting hall, the circuit court, church, and school. Mary White was the Sunday School and day school teacher. Nine children attended this school in the first year.
The building served as the first school for 15 years. 1835 The Anishnaabek needed a treaty to stay in Michigan. In the fall of 1835. Odawa from the Little Traverse, Grand River, Grand Traverse, & Muskegon, along with Ojibway from Sault Ste.
Marie and Mackinac, traveled to Washington, DC for treaty negotiations. Henry School Schoolcraft, Indian Agent for the Michigan Territory, handled treaty negotiations on behalf of the United States. Many Anishnaabek did not trust Schoolcraft. Negotiations went on for weeks.
Each group of Anishnaabek expressed the wishes of their communities, who hoped to retain their tradition lands and receive government annuities. The United States wanted Anishnaabek land. The Odawa & Ojibway agreed to cede over 13 million acres of land to the United States. In return, the Treaty of Washington guaranteed permanent reservation lands and access to natural resources.
Including hunting and fishing rights. The United States agreed to pay for the land and provide additional services. The Anishnaabek left Washington confident they had avoided forced removal.
Source

04-Local-History/Grand-River-Newspaper-D.title: Grand River Newspaper — Description of Grand Haven Grand Haven, the county seat of O
04-Local-History/Grand-River-Newspaper-D.content:
Grand River Newspaper — Description of Grand Haven Grand Haven, the county seat of O
1852
Description of Grand Haven Grand Haven, the county seat of Ottawa County Mich., 213 miles West bank of the Grand River, half a mile from the entrance into Lake Michigan between which and the Lake are sand hills 200’ in height Its harbor (the best on this side of the Lake) could be made by construction of piers superior to any in the upper great lakes, and with such an improvement by the general government, would open to the Interior of the state by rail and plank roads to the Rapids, a channel for the outlet of a vast amount of produce, the staples of a soil abounding in agricultural and mineral wealth, and the inlet of the products of the world abroad.--- At the present writing there is from 10 to 13 feet depth of water in the channel, which is indicated with lights and guides established at the mouth of the river. Grand Haven contains a Court House which is also used as a church, a jail, a schoolhouse with spacious rooms above and below, with a cupola and bell, a beautiful edifice which cost nearly $2,000, and accommodates over 100 scholars pursuing the various branches of education, under accomplished teachers, open to all classes of youth, including the penniless as well as the rich. There are 3 large public houses, well sustained, one of which, the Washington, is three stories high with a hall in the attic, occupied by the Odd Fellows. There are five stores, three forwarding houses, two shops, several groceries, a large tannery, tailor shop, blacksmith and carpenter shops and several fisheries.
The principal businesses of the place is the manufacture and shipment of lumber. The number of steam and water mills for that purpose within the range of navigation here, and in this part of the country is fourteen, five only of which are water mills, the remainder mostly double steam mills, which average 20,000 feet in 24 hours. The quantities of lumber shipped from the port this season will amount to nearly or quite 30.000,000 feet besides a proportional amount of shingles, shingle-bolts, lath, wood cedar posts, bark, etc. Heavy shipments of wheat, flour and plaster have been made this season, and a large amount of merchandise received for this place and the various points in Ottawa, Kent and Ionia.
There are two physicians and no lawyers. The population of the county is 6,480, embracing the Holland Colony, twenty miles south of the county seat, on Black River, another good harbor when improved by the government. The population of this village and Mill Point is about 1,000.
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 46.

Grand River Newspaper — Grand Haven, Michigan A sad accident happened to Henry Mathe…
1852
Grand Haven, Michigan A sad accident happened to Henry Mather, on Friday of last week, while at work in Ferry’s steam mill near this place. He went below among the gearing for the purpose of clearing away the saw dust from some of the machinery, when the skirt of his coat was caught under a band which whirled him around the shaft some sixty times, before the machinery was effectually stopped, breaking his leg twice in two, and tearing the flesh badly from the other leg, breaking his ribs, and otherwise injuring him. His left leg is so badly broken, it was deemed necessary to amputate it, which operation was well and skillfully performed by our excellent surgeons Monroe and Tuttle. The sufferer will live under their charge, if skill and attention will save him GRAND RIVER NEWSPAPER Grand Haven, Michigan DIED Henry Colt Mather, the young man that was injured at Ferry’s Mill, of which mention was made in the paper of the 13th inst., in consequence of the injuries received, on the afternoon of Thursday, the 15th inst.
His friends, though absent, are assured that everything, both medical and the care of his acquaintances here, Was done for his comfort that sympathy and judgement dictated.

Grand River Newspaper — Grand Haven, Michigan Charles Dushane, a Frenchman, residing…
1852
Grand Haven, Michigan Charles Dushane, a Frenchman, residing in this village, was stabbed in the breast, by an Indian, on Thursday last. It appears that the Indian who had just arrived in town by the steamer Algoma, from Grand Rapids, called at the bar of one of the groceries in town, for whiskey----when he was told in English by the young man attending, that he could have none. Mr Dushane, who stood by the young man, interpreted the refusal of whiskey, when the Indian drew his knife And stabbed Mr. Dushane, and ran for the woods south of the village.
He was pursued by Sheriff Scott and several others, and in a half hour was taken and lodged in jail. Mr. D. is said to have received only a flesh wound.
The weather has not been sufficiently warm to dissipate the snow in our village which fell on Monday, the 5th. Such an intrusion of old winter to mid spring, has not been since 1843. Our farmers are obligated to “fodder” with the same diligence that winter necessarily requires, and we are gratified to learn that none have suffered for the article that can make “cuds” of. We have a state of weather now breaking in permanent spring.

Van Raalte attracted government attention to the need for harbor improvements. Following recommendations from a government engineer, Congress appropriated funds to open the channel so steamboats could dock at the site President Franklin Pierce vetoed the bill, so the settlers grabbed their tools and deepened the channel to allow shallow draft vessels into Blake Lake.
In 1853 the electors of Grand Haven authorized insurance in bonds to raise money to build a railroad bridge over the Grand River. It caused the former DVD & M RR, a predecessor to the Grand Trunk RR to come to Grand Haven where the Depot sits at the bottom of Washington. The area at the foot of Dewey Hill was abandoned. It was gradually overrun by the sand dune.
When the RR ceased its terminus in Grand Haven its land reverted to the City of as the bond terms provided.

04-Local-History/Jul-3-Grand-Rapids-Eagl.title: Jul 3 Grand Rapids Eagle Newspaper
04-Local-History/Jul-3-Grand-Rapids-Eagl.content:
Jul 3 Grand Rapids Eagle Newspaper
1857
GRAND HAVEN HAS UNDERGROUND RAILROAD The underground railroad was a organized system designed to help runaway slaves find safety in Canada and slave-free states. Residences of sympathetic white propl were used as “safe houses”, but since slaves were designated by law as property, harboring them was considered a crime, although offenders were not often prosecuted in the free states. Grand Haven was long rumored to have had a safe house, and there is concrete reference to its existence in the Eagle Newspaper: “U.G.R.R. a passenger by the Underground Railway passed through Grand Haven the week before last.” Although some detail of his condition was cited, the fugatives name was not revealed.
Readers were informed that he arrived in Grand Haven and boarded a boat headed for Grand Rapids. “The Captain raised a suit of clothes and $7.00 in cash, and he was furnished with the best directions to the Canada shore were we trust he arrived in safety.”

04-Local-History/Railway-Bridge-1858.title: Railway Bridge
04-Local-History/Railway-Bridge-1858.content:
Railway Bridge
1858
Grand Haven, MI The Detroit & Milwaukee Railway built the first bridge over the Grand River To connect Detroit with the Lake Michigan port of Grand Haven. The Railway made its way to the mouth of the Grand River, staying on the north side of the river, to avoid the expense of building of a bridge. A depot , hotel, restaurants, and small businesses soon developed at the foot of Dewy Hill. Passengers and freight were ferried across the river.
Twelve years later, a bridge was built, and the railroad came directly into Grand Haven 1858 Located in the Village, the lumber stretched from the banks of Spring Lake to the foot of Division Street and west to the railroad bridge. They did not formally incorporate their partnership until 1863. The firm had several mills in the area, including the Hopkin’s Mill, which they purchased and then added on more buildings to increase the mill’s processing capacity. Culter and Savage also maintained a mill further west on Spring Lake, near the current location of Old Boy’s Brewhouse.
The firm later purchased the Haire & Tilford mill on Grand River in 1870. The company became a powerhouse in the lumber business, continuing to work in the Spring lake area until the lumber industry dried up in the 1890’s due to massive deforestation. Once the decline occurred, the company moved to Ontario, Canada.
Source

04-Local-History/Rix-Robison-1827.title: Rix Robison
04-Local-History/Rix-Robison-1827.content:
Rix Robison
1827
Gobemouche [Grand Haven] was the headquarters of the 20 trading posts established by the American Fur Company, with Mr. Robinson as their agent and sole manager. The trading posts commenced at Kalamazoo in the south, extending to Little Traverse Bay in the North. The headquarter buildings were quite respectable in appearance.
The trading post had a store, warehouse with a pole dock and a dwelling house with 4 rooms, occupied by Mr. Robinson and his wife (a half-bred woman) and a clerk. The clerk was a 18 year old boy, who came to Grand Haven and took charge of the trading post. He had no knowledge of French or Indian languages.
He had as helpers or aids, 4 voyagers and one half-breed girl as his interpreter and housekeeper, who had been educated at the mission school in Mackinaw. In Mr. Robinson’s absence, which was the larger portion of the time, the dwelling was occupied by the clerk and housekeeper, whoever she might be. It happened in this case to be a very pretty girl, whom Mr.
Robinson was extremely anxious to marry to the clerk.

04-Local-History/Spring-Lake-House-1871.title: Spring Lake House
04-Local-History/Spring-Lake-House-1871.content:
Spring Lake House
1871
Spring Lake, MI Professor Alexander Winchell from the University of Michigan was a quest of spring lake resident and lumber baron Hunter Savidge early in 1870. Winchell believed that there were salt deposits under the entire state. With that theory in mind, Hunter partnered with Aloys Bilz, Allen Adsit, 7 Robert Haire to organize the Spring Lake Salt Company. This business was located next to Hopkins Mill site, north of Liberty St.
The owners bought drilling equipment from the Hopkins & Hancock Sawmill and commenced boring for salt. Instead, they found magnetic mineral springs at the depth of 200’ . The company disbanded and the next year the same group of 4 reunited to build the Spring Lake House, an impressive spa, to take advantage of the spring’s medicinal effects. The resort was located roughly between Culter and Rex and North Liberty St., extending to the shores of Spring Lake.
Just to the west was the Culter & Savidge sawmill. The hotel, $70,000 to build, consisted of 74 rooms, with another 30 rooms in adjoining cottages, providing room for another 250 guests. Bowling and billiards were also offered. The grounds were made attractive by the addition of fountains, flowers, shade trees and well-trimmed lawn.
The bathhouse, built over the spring, was nearby. The owners claimed, “Bathing In this water was a luxury” . “It is perfectly cleansing without soap and remarkably strengthening. ” In another advertisement they added, “The waters of this Spring have gained a great reputation.
However, a letter printed in a Grand Haven newspaper on July 4, 1872, shed a contrary view: “Your correspondent visited the famous Spring Lake well a few days since, swallowed some goblets of blackish water which is pumped out of the bowels of the earth for healing of Spring Lakers. They seem to consider it without making faces, but all look very serious as the gulp down the slightly salty, insipid liquid. The hotel was destroyed by fire on June 16, 1916, and never rebuild. The drawing of the hotel is dated 1882.
The flyer was date 1880.
Source

04-Local-History/Traveling-Conditions-fo.title: Traveling Conditions for Immigrants Migrating to the America on Ship
04-Local-History/Traveling-Conditions-fo.content:
Traveling Conditions for Immigrants Migrating to the America on Ship
1800
At the beginning of the 1900th century, passengers were seen as a sideline for cargo ships, as a way to increase their funds. This would Have been a very cheap way to travel, but also very uncomfortable. Overcrowding and unsanitary conditions were commonplace. Those able to pay for a ticket travelled on the upper decks called 1st class, and the cheaper ticket passenger on the lower decks called steerage.
Steerage generally had shared living and communal cooking arrangements. Tiny living quarters with often only a blanket or canvas curtain as a divider. In fact, in the early phase of emigration the living areas would be made temporary so that on the return voyage the partitions could be removed, and the area used for storing cargo. Fresh air and light would be minimal, portholes were shut during bad weather to prevent water getting into the living quarters, and the hatches or trap doors to steerage would often be locked during storm weather.
This posed a greater risk for emigrants as they would be trapped if a fire broke out. Steerage passengers would sleep in bunks, often very narrow and tightly packed together. Often,, they were required to bring their own mattresses and blankets. Dining tables were often temporary affairs, designed to be hung up when not in use.
Space was in such short supply that often passengers found themselves eating on the bunks. SLEEPING QUARTERS On most ships Steerage was made up of 3 sections, single men, married couples and single women. One description, being of a sleeping compartment about 14 feet by 12 feetlong and 8 feet high. The space inside would be very cramped, with often only a narrow alley between the bunks for one person to walk along at any given time, with no space for passing.
This would house 24 people; each had a berth about 2 feet wide. Darkness, dampness and stale air would be commonplace. The smell of vomit, and unemptied chamber pots, restricted movement and lack of sunlight would have added to the feeling of claustrophobia. Seasickness, lack of privacy and inadequate food made for a miserable voyage.
ILLNESS It would take 4 weeks to travel to North America, plenty of time for passengers to fall ill. Although all passengers had t pass a physical exam upon boarding to ensure all travelers were healthy and to prevent the spread of disease, sickness was inevitable. Common illnesses at the time were marasmus, diarrhea, scarlet fever, tuberculosis, bronchial conditions made worse by the icy temperatures and dampness. Constant sea sickness culminated in malnutrition for those who could not keep their food down and the lack of privacy led to the spread of disease.
Many passengers initially found it difficult to sleep due to the swaying of the ship during storms, the jostling of strong waves made even standing up difficult. FOOD Before regulations were in place, there was not a large variety of food and water was not fresh for those in steerage. Water was measured out and used sparingly. The meals would have depended on the skill of the cook and the ingredients available.
On early ships food would be cooked by passengers in communal areas. Which would be challenging on rough seas.
Source

History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families by Ruth Taber, 25 Dec 2025, page 22.

09-Research-Log/Open-Questions.title: Open Questions
09-Research-Log/Open-Questions.content:
Open Questions & Research Gaps

Living document. Add a question whenever the source is ambiguous, missing data, or contradictory. Link from the relevant person/place/event note so questions surface in backlinks.

Source-document anomalies caught during Phase 2 extraction
These are places where the source PDF appears to contain typos or inconsistencies that should be verified against original records:

William VerBerkmoes (b. 12 Mar 1888) — source lists his parents as “Eugene A Simmons & Francis Adle VerBerkmoes,” which are actually his sister’s husband and his sister. ✓ RESOLVED — corrected via _scripts/people_corrections.json to William Felix Adriaansz VerBerkmoes & Sarah Janette Leendertsd Faas (PDF p. 166).
Adrian VerBerkmoes (b. 16 Mar 1880) — gen 7. Source lists his parents as “Adriaansz Willemsz VerBerkmoes & Derkje Adriaansd Schippers,” but they are his grandparents. ✓ RESOLVED — corrected to Adriaan Adriaansz VerBerkmoes & Elizabeth Johanna Rogge (PDF p. 166).
Susan A VerBerkmoes (b. Jul 1881) — same parent issue as above. ✓ RESOLVED — corrected to the same parents as Adrian (PDF p. 166).
Ruth Louise Snoek (b. 2 Jan 1922) — source lists her parents as “Adriaan Adriaansz VerBerkmoes & Elisabeth Johanna Rogge,” but those are her great-grandparents. ✓ RESOLVED — corrected to John Orren Snoek & Delia (Derka) VerBerkmoes (PDF p. 185).
Several gen-12 entries on p. 174 (“name Damp,” “name Ranft,” etc.) are placeholders for unrecorded children — names should be filled in if/when known.


The four corrections above are applied automatically every time generate_notes.py runs. The original (incorrect) source values are preserved in each affected person note’s ## Source footer for verification, with a ⚠️ warning marker so the correction is visible in the rendered note.

Dates needing confirmation

Anna Samargia — birth village given as “Beljevine, Croatia.” Spelling should be verified (likely Beljanovo or similar).
Adriaan Adriaansz VerBerkmoes (1849–1924) — source p. 61 gives death date as “Dec 18 or 28 1870” for the father; Adriaan himself died Jul 13 1924.
Pieter Jacobus Andriaansz VerBerkmoes — source gives “b. Dec 7, 1851 or Dec 6, 1852” for the same person. Needs original record.

People mentioned but with no detail
People who appear in the source as a name only, without dates, places, or parents recorded. These are excellent targets for follow-up research:

To be populated once Phase 3 enrichment surfaces all such mentions in the timeline pages.

Lines requiring deeper research

Samargia line — only the immigrant generation (Anna, b. 1908) is documented. Her parents, siblings, and Croatian background are missing.
Earliest VerBerkmoes (1g, 2g) — Jacobus VerBerkmoes & Johanna E Weist have no dates or places; only that they were the founding couple.
Earliest Snoek (1g) — Jan Snoek & Jantien Arends similarly have no dates.

How to use this file
When you find an answer, don’t delete the question — strike it through and add the resolution underneath, with the source. That way the trail of research is preserved.

index.title: Snoek–VerBerkmoes Family History
index.content:
Snoek–VerBerkmoes Family History
A research vault deconstructed from Ruth Taber’s History of the Coffin, Samargia, Snoek, VerBerkmoes Families (25 Dec 2025). Over 1,800 interlinked notes covering four family lines from 1425 to 2023 — England, Zeeland, Drenthe, Croatia, and finally Grand Haven, Michigan.

We are the chosen. In each family, there is one who seems called to find the ancestors. To put flesh on their bones and make them live again. To tell the family story and to feel that somehow, they know and approve. We are the storytellers of the tribe.
— Opening of the source document
